clue.text: Sort of chicken one American dispatched: hard to clean, I suspect

indicators.note: dispatched means sent away, so the one American letter is taken out of the pool before rearranging
suspect as an adjective means dodgy or not to be trusted, so the letters before it are not in their proper order

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for American; one such letter goes

explanation.surface: A wry aside on the US practice of washing chicken carcasses that are hard to get clean, a sore point in UK trade talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' rearranges HARD TO CLEAN I once 'one American dispatched' has removed one A from that pool.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken washed in a chlorine solution is the American poultry the British press made infamous during trade-deal debates.

clue.text: Movie star Dance stifles scream

indicators.note: to stifle something is to smother it, so the dance closes around the other piece

parts.note: the Charleston is a lively 1920s dance
a scream is something hilarious, which makes you laugh

explanation.surface: A film star at a dance trying to hold back a scream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stifles' is the container signal. 'scream' means something hilarious, as in 'he's a scream', not a shriek of fear.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Laughton was an English actor famous in Hollywood films such as Mutiny on the Bounty.

clue.text: Rugby players from Pwllheli on stand-by

indicators.note: from says the answer is taken straight out of the run of letters in the words that follow

explanation.surface: Rugby players from a Welsh seaside town waiting on the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' lifts the letters out of PwllheLI ON Stand-by. Pwllheli is a small town in north Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The British and Irish touring rugby union side, picked from the four home nations, is known by this big-cat nickname.

clue.text: Fix resistance in stereo output

indicators.note: in places the resistance letter inside the rearranged letters
output, as in what a stereo produces, is read as the letters of stereo being put out in a new order

parts.note: R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A repair job on the resistance in a hi-fi's output stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'output' rearranges STEREO to make ESTORE, and 'in' puts R inside it after the first E.
explanation.definitionFit: To fix something broken is to repair it, bringing it back to its former condition.

clue.text: Scored having picked up fellow outside gallery

indicators.note: outside says the reversed fellow sits around the gallery
in a down clue, picked up means lifted from bottom to top, so the letters read upwards

parts.note: a don is a fellow of a university college
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: Someone scored after collecting a friend outside an art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'picked up' reads upwards, and 'outside' splits the reversed piece around the gallery. 'Scored' sounds like sport but is musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Music that is scored has been written down in notation, so the two past participles match.

clue.text: Without hesitation, posted online message, forgetting wife was unstable?

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the other letters go around the hesitation
forgetting means leaving out, so the wife letter is dropped

parts.note: to tweet is to post a short message online
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A spouse posts something online without a pause, forgets their partner, and wonders if they were losing their balance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forgetting' leaves TEETED, and 'Without' is the old sense of outside. 'Without hesitation' reads as 'promptly' but is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To teeter is to wobble on the verge of falling, so the past tense matches being unsteady.

clue.text: Album from Yes, perhaps

parts.note: definitely is an emphatic way to say yes
perhaps means maybe

explanation.surface: A record that might be labelled as yes, or perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words contradict each other, which is the joke of the record's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1994 debut record by the Manchester band Oasis carries this contradictory title.

clue.text: Ring jokers writing about contracted setters Sri Lanka has

indicators.note: contracted means shortened, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: circa is the Latin for about, used in writing before approximate dates
the setters of a puzzle can refer to themselves as us
CL is the international vehicle registration code for Sri Lanka
to own something is to have it

explanation.surface: Comic performers write about the compilers whom Sri Lanka has in its grip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contracted' shortens CIRCA to CIRC. 'Ring' is the arena under the big top, not jewellery or a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: Clowns are jokers who perform in a big-top ring, the arena of a travelling show.

clue.text: Renovated house with angelic sofa

indicators.note: a renovated building has been done up, so these letters are made over into a new order

explanation.surface: A done-up house with a heavenly sofa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Renovated' rearranges HOUSE plus ANGELIC; 'with' joins the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: This French term names a long upholstered seat with a back at one end, a kind of couch for reclining.

clue.text: Mother leaves behind the first idealised representations in the unconscious

indicators.note: behind places the mother and leaves pieces after the first piece

parts.note: the first can be I, the Roman numeral one
ma is an informal word for mother
leaves means departs, goes

explanation.surface: Mother departs, leaving the first one behind her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' is a charade order signal: the mother and leaves pieces trail the Roman numeral one, which is 'the first'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Jungian psychology an imago is an idealised mental image of a person, such as a parent, held in the unconscious mind.

clue.text: Will's night flight flew there, partly travelling west

indicators.note: travelling west says the hidden letters are read backwards
partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A night on which an aircraft flew somewhere, heading westward for part of the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' picks HTFLEWT from fligHT FLEW There and 'travelling west' reads it right to left. Will is William Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's comedy Twelfth Night completes the phrase, so this ordinal is Will's night.

clue.text: Bloomer by Labour leader once, having upset 62.5% of Scotland first

indicators.note: first says this piece comes before the Labour leader in the answer
upset means knocked over, so the selected letters are tipped into a new order
62.5% is five eighths, so the first five of the eight letters of Scotland are taken

parts.note: Michael Foot led the Labour Party from 1980 to 1983

explanation.surface: A former Labour leader's gaffe that offended much of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 62.5% is five eighths of an eight-letter word; 'upset' rearranges that pick and 'first' places it at the front. 'Bloomer' is a flower, not a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a flowering plant; this yellow-flowered weed is one.

clue.text: Boring state of affairs, if repackaged Penguin but no PG …

indicators.note: repackaged means put into new wrapping, so the letters are rearranged
but no says these two letters are taken out of the pool first

parts.note: PG is a film rating, parental guidance, taken as its two letters

explanation.surface: A dull situation, like a Penguin paperback reissued without its film-rating sticker.
explanation.walkthrough: Take P and G out of PENGUIN ('but no PG') and 'repackaged' rearranges the rest, ENUIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is listless weariness from lack of interest, the condition of being bored.

clue.text: … Tips from shopping online (service only average)

indicators.note: tips are the very ends of things, here the initial letters of the following words

explanation.surface: Online shopping service rated just average, following on from the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips from' takes the first letter of each of the four words. The ellipsis just links the surface to the previous clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something middling, neither good nor bad, is mediocre or average.

clue.text: Note following late small change at the very heart of things

indicators.note: following puts the note after the other two pieces

parts.note: late can mean dead, as in the late king
a cent is a small coin
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A note comes after a recent bit of loose change, at the core of affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' sets the note last; 'at' is a link word, leaving the noun phrase as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The exact middle point of something is its absolute core, the very heart.

clue.text: TV programme doctors watch outside store, briefly

indicators.note: outside says the rearranged letters wrap around the shortened store
to doctor is to tamper with, so the letters of watch are rearranged
briefly means cut short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a shop is a store

explanation.surface: Doctors watch television outside a shop for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doctors' rearranges WATCH into CHATW and 'briefly' trims the store; 'outside' wraps one around the other. 'doctors' looks like a noun but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A chat show is a television format where a host interviews guests, so it is a kind of broadcast.

clue.text: Plunges steeply, demolishing vicar's shed

indicators.note: demolishing means knocking down, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Someone tearing down a clergyman's garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'demolishing' rearranges the letters of VICARS SHED.
explanation.definitionFit: A submarine that crash-dives descends very rapidly in an emergency, so it plunges steeply.

clue.text: See 7
Puck's old hat? Deadlock ensues …

parts.note: Puck is the setter of this puzzle, so Puck's means I am, contracted to I'm
old hat means out of date, passe

explanation.surface: The setter wonders if they are past it, and a stalemate follows.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym is Puck, so 'Puck's' is the setter saying I'M. The ellipsis just links to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadlock is a situation where no progress can be made, a stalemate.

clue.text: … before real ire is dissipated

indicators.note: dissipated means scattered, so the letters of the two words are dispersed and reassembled

explanation.surface: Continuing from the deadlock, before genuine anger fades away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dissipated' rearranges REAL IRE; 'is' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: As adverbs, both mean at a previous time, sooner than now.

clue.text: Airline allegedly a little under 50% at fault

indicators.note: at fault means in the wrong, so the selected letters are put in a new order
four of the nine letters is a little under half, so the first four letters of the word are taken

explanation.surface: An airline supposedly slightly less than half to blame for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'allegedly' looks like a comment on the claim but is the source word; 'a little under 50%' takes ALLE, which 'at fault' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: El Al is the national flag carrier of Israel.

clue.text: See 8
Cycling hard? This suggests duty or obligation, perhaps

definitions.text: This suggests duty or obligation, perhaps

indicators.note: cycling means going round, so the last letter wheels round to the front

parts.note: tough means hard

explanation.surface: A question whether hard cycling is really a duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' moves the H of TOUGH to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: This modal verb, as in 'you should', expresses what someone is obliged or morally bound to do.

clue.text: Somebody that's eaten one midsummer fruit

indicators.note: something eaten is taken inside, so the person surrounds the other letters

parts.note: a person is somebody
I is the Roman numeral for one
the middle of summer is its two central letters

explanation.surface: Someone who has eaten a single fruit in high summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's eaten' is the container signal; 'midsummer' is read literally as the middle of the word summer.
explanation.definitionFit: The persimmon is an orange, tomato-like fruit of an Asian tree, also called sharon fruit.

clue.text: Question dropping leader from paper

indicators.note: dropping the leader means losing the first letter

parts.note: tissue is a thin soft paper

explanation.surface: A query that has been cut from the top of a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping leader from' removes the T from TISSUE. 'leader' hints at a newspaper editorial, but it is just the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is a point in dispute or a matter under discussion, a question.

clue.text: Scores from shot centre half has left, mistakenly

indicators.note: mistakenly means wrongly, so the letters are arranged in the wrong order
half has left means only one half of the word remains, here the front three letters of centre

explanation.surface: A football commentary: the centre half has gone off, and goals came from a wayward shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half has left' keeps CEN, the first half of CENTRE; 'mistakenly' rearranges SHOT plus CEN. 'centre half' looks like the football position.
explanation.definitionFit: Notches are small cuts used to keep a tally, so they are marks scored in a count.

clue.text: Critically shocked expression after playing short suit okay

indicators.note: playing means fooling about, so the letters are moved around
short means cut off at the end, so the last letter of suit goes

explanation.surface: A card game where the short suit is played after a gasp of disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' drops the last letter of the suit and 'playing' rearranges the pool; 'after' is a link word. 'short suit' looks like bridge jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: An exasperated exclamation of disapproval, roughly 'honestly, can you believe it', voiced when critical of something.

clue.text: Time to chuck out the old verse? Aye, it might be

definitions.text: Time to chuck out the old

parts.note: read as wordplay, the first word of the solution signals a new arrangement of the remaining eight letters, which rearrange to make verse and aye

explanation.surface: A night for ditching the past, perhaps an old poem; yes, it could be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it might be' says the solution, taken as wordplay, could produce 'verse? Aye': NEW, a common anagram signal, acting on YEARSEVE.
explanation.definitionFit: The last night of December is when people see off the outgoing twelve months.
